JWST-SPARK, second round: the level-1 question, what stays empty, and NIRCam¶

This report follows JWST-SPARK on ten MIRI datasets (2026-10-30). It covers four pieces of work:

  • settling the open question about one kind of level-1 pixel;
  • finding out what the MIRI images still leave empty, and which methods could fill it;
  • a change to the PSF fill;
  • a first NIRCam version of the package.

The package is at https://github.com/tyoo37/JWST-SPARK. The W51 copy (satrestore/) follows it.

Summary

  • The level-1 question is settled. The method stays, and the error now says how far these pixels can be trusted.
    • Some pixels are flagged only because a neighbour saturated, and then look like level-1 pixels.
    • Neighbours flagged from group 3 or 4 can be checked against their own groups read before the neighbour saturated. There the level-1 correction agrees with them to within −0.04 to +0.045 dex (figure 1), so the correction itself is not biased for neighbour pixels.
    • The large gaps seen before (0.1–0.2 dex) are extra charge that the saturating neighbour adds to the later groups.
    • A smaller gap to the first increment remains: 0.04–0.12 dex, and it does not vanish when the neighbour saturates late (figure 2). These pixels now carry that measured gap in their error (ERR), dataset by dataset.
    • In W51 this changes the ERR of 4,942–104,133 pixel-exposures per filter. Values and dither checks stay the same.
  • Faint isolated pixels drift from the level-1 relation, and the drift does not matter here.
    • The drift is up to ±0.05 dex at 4,000–6,000 DN.
    • Neighbour pixels of the same brightness do not drift.
    • 85–100% of the pixels the correction serves are brighter than 6,000 DN. No drift correction was added.
  • What the MIRI images still leave empty.
    • Empty: 141,364 saturated sky pixels in the ten mosaics. 88% of them are in gc3571 F1500W and ngc6334 F2550W and F2100W.
    • 77% have every group above the top of the response curve, so their ramps hold no usable information.
    • The other 23% get a curve value outside the range the curve was tested on.
    • 99% sit in regions too large for the PSF fill.
  • Methods that could fill the empty area. Another MIRI filter of the same sky can reach 86% of the empty area.
    • Scaling it by the colour measured on a ring around each hole predicts hidden test pixels to an rms of 0.04 dex (gc3571 F1500W) and 0.10 dex (ngc6334), but only 0.18–0.32 dex in the smaller sets.
    • Inpainting gives 0.10–0.33 dex and often falls below the saturation level.
    • Other dithers and other programs on disk add nothing.
    • The literature survey points the same way: fill from shorter exposures or other filters, with the method recorded for each pixel. It also warns against inpainting photometry.
    • The package does not have such a fill yet; it is the recommended next step (section 6).
  • PSF fill.
    • The fit now uses a box of 4 pixels around the core instead of 12, and the model is integrated over each detector pixel.
    • Against the response curve, ngc6334 F2100W went from +0.16 to +0.008 dex and gc3571 F1500W from +0.065 to +0.041. PSF fills now switch on in both.
    • At F770W the fit still reads 0.13–0.20 dex too bright, so the fills there stay off.
    • The gate now uses the worst self-test bin. Where no curve value exists to compare with, the bin must be within 0.02 dex.
  • The ten MIRI datasets, rerun with the final package. The share of saturated sky with a value moved by at most 0.3 percentage points. Restored values moved by a median of 0.001–0.006 dex (95% within 0.010 dex), from the robust level-1 fit. The other changes are in the error column and the PSF gates.
  • NIRCam, first version.
    • The package now runs on NIRCam, one detector at a time, using per-pixel saturation levels from CRDS. It was tested on six datasets: four readout patterns, 2–7 groups, and short and long wavelengths.
    • NIRCam's first group has no pedestal, so the level-1 correction moves values by 0.015 dex or less.
    • PSF fills pass the stricter gate in two of the six sets.
    • The large NIRCam gains (group 0 of neighbour-flagged pixels, the ZEROFRAME) need work that is listed in section 6.
  • Two safeguards came from NIRCam:
    • Robust level-1 fit. One unflagged pixel with an impossible rate pulled one exposure's fit to a = 0.002 against 0.75 expected. The fit now ignores such points, and each fit must pass its own self-test.
    • No lost pipeline values. The first NIRCam version dropped pipeline values that come from the ZEROFRAME. It now keeps them, and every run counts any pipeline value it loses.

Glossary

term meaning
group one of the successive reads of the detector during an integration
level-1 pixel a pixel whose first group is good and whose second group is flagged saturated; its rate comes from the first group alone
level-1 correction the rate from the first group, (lin0 − b) / (a × group time), with a and b measured on pixels that have 2–4 good groups
flagged by a neighbour the pipeline also flags the 8 neighbours of a saturated pixel from that group on, even when their own signal is lower
increment the signal a pixel gains between two groups
extra charge (spill) charge that a pixel next to a saturating one collects beyond its own sky signal
response curve MIRI's raw signal keeps rising slowly past saturation; the package learns this curve from the dataset and reads it backwards
curve top the charge where the response curve flattens; beyond it the ramp holds no information
PSF fill the shape of a point source (STPSF model) fitted to the measured pixels around a saturated core
self-test hiding measured pixels of the same data and predicting them; its median is the bias, its half-width the scatter
local ratio another filter's image, scaled by the ratio of the two filters on a ring around the hole
inpainting filling a hole by smooth interpolation from its edge (here biharmonic)
ZEROFRAME NIRCam's first single frame, stored separately when a group averages several frames
dex a factor of 10 in log units: 0.1 dex is a factor of 1.26, 0.01 dex 2.3%
ERR the uncertainty (dex) the package writes for each restored pixel

1. Level-1 pixels flagged by a neighbour¶

The question. A pixel can be flagged saturated in group 1 only because a neighbour saturated there, while its own signal stays below saturation. The package gives it the level-1 correction from its first group. Against its own later groups, that value read 0.05–0.2 dex low. Was the correction biased for these pixels, or do the later groups carry extra charge from the saturating neighbour?

The test. Pixels flagged from group 3 or 4 by a neighbour have good groups taken before that neighbour saturated, which hold no extra charge from a saturated pixel. If the level-1 correction works for neighbour pixels, it should agree with those groups.

Figure 1 compares the level-1 value with a measured rate.

  • Left panel: isolated pixels, with no saturated neighbour.
  • Right panel: neighbour pixels, against their groups read before the neighbour saturated.
  • Grey band: ±0.04 dex.
  • Bars at the bottom: where the pixels the correction actually serves lie in brightness.

What the figure shows:

  • Neighbour pixels (right) stay within −0.04 to +0.045 dex across 2,000–20,000 DN, and within −0.04 to +0.01 dex above 4,000 DN.
  • Isolated pixels (left) drift at low brightness. At 4,000–6,000 DN, three of the four F770W test sets go up by +0.04 to +0.05 dex; W51 goes down by −0.05 dex.
  • Served pixels sit almost entirely above 6,000 DN, where both groups agree. The drift therefore does not affect restored values, and no drift correction was added.
In [2]:
def parse_spill(path):
    # the text output of satrestore_tests/diag_l1spill.py
    num = lambda s: float('nan') if 'nan' in s else float(s)
    A, B, C, D = [], [], [], {}
    for line in open(path):
        m = re.match(r'\s+X\s+(\d+)-\s*(\d+): ([+-]?[\d.]+|[+ ]*nan) \((\d+)', line)
        if m:
            A.append((int(m[1]), int(m[2]), num(m[3]), int(m[4])))
        m = re.match(r'\s+increment\s+(\d+)-\s*(\d+): B ([+-]?[\d.]+|[+ ]*nan) \((\d+)\), A ([+-]?[\d.]+|[+ ]*nan) \((\d+)\)', line)
        if m:
            B.append((int(m[1]), int(m[2]), num(m[3]), int(m[4]), num(m[5]), int(m[6])))
        m = re.search(r'X\s+(\d+)-\s*(\d+), f ([\d.]+)-([\d.]+): n\s+(\d+)\s+gap0 ([+-][\d.]+)\s+gap1 ([+-][\d.]+)\s+gap0 if all spill ([+-][\d.]+)', line)
        if m:
            C.append(tuple(float(m[i]) for i in range(1, 9)))
        m = re.search(r' D, level 1: n (\d+),.*?: ([\d.]+) / ([\d.]+) / ([\d.]+); percentiles 5/50/95 \[\s*([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\]', line)
        if m:
            D = dict(n=int(m[1]), below6000=float(m[4]), p5=float(m[5]), p50=float(m[6]), p95=float(m[7]))
    return (pd.DataFrame(A, columns=['lo', 'hi', 'd', 'n']), pd.DataFrame(B, columns=['lo', 'hi', 'B', 'nB', 'A', 'nA']),
            pd.DataFrame(C, columns=['xlo', 'xhi', 'flo', 'fhi', 'n', 'gap0', 'gap1', 'pred']), D)

          'W51_F770W': 'W51 F770W', 'W51_F1000W': 'W51 F1000W', 'W51_F2100W': 'W51 F2100W'}
SP = {k: parse_spill(f'{O}/level1/spill2_{k}.log') for k in L1SETS}

for k, lab in L1SETS.items():

    ax[0].plot(np.sqrt(a.lo * a.hi), a.d, color=COL[k], marker='o', ms=4, label=lab)
    b = B[np.isfinite(B.B) & (B.nB >= 30)]
    ax[1].plot(np.sqrt(b.lo * b.hi), b.B, color=COL[k], marker='o', ms=5, label=lab)
    if D:
        y = -0.26 - 0.022 * list(L1SETS).index(k)
        for a_ in ax:
            a_.plot([D['p5'], D['p95']], [y, y], color=COL[k], lw=3, solid_capstyle='butt', alpha=0.8)
for a_, t in zip(ax, ['isolated pixels (no saturated neighbour)', 'pixels flagged by a neighbour that saturated in group 3 or 4']):
    a_.axhspan(-0.04, 0.04, color=LIGHT, zorder=0); a_.axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=1)
    a_.set_xscale('log'); a_.set_xlim(300, 1e5); a_.set_ylim(-0.42, 0.55); a_.set_title(t)
ax[0].set_xlabel('charge per group from the full ramp, X (DN)'); ax[1].set_xlabel('charge per group before the neighbour saturated (DN)')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

When does the extra charge start? Figure 2 follows the group-1 neighbours. The x-axis is when, between the group-0 and group-1 reads, the neighbour crossed saturation. That time is estimated from the neighbour's own first group and level-1 rate.

  • Red: the level-1 value against the later increment (group 1 to 2). It sits 0.09–0.23 dex below, at every time.
  • Blue: the level-1 value against the first increment (group 0 to 1). It sits 0.04–0.12 dex below.
  • Dashed: what the first increment would show if the extra charge began exactly when the neighbour crossed saturation. It shrinks toward 0 when the neighbour saturates late.

The measured gap shrinks much less than the dashed line. Two readings fit this:

  • the neighbour passes charge on before it reaches the saturation flag level;
  • part of the gap is a bias of the level-1 value for these pixels.

The first test (figure 1, right) limits that bias to 0.04 dex or less, at least where the neighbour saturates later. The package therefore keeps the level-1 value and adds the measured gap to these pixels' error. The gap is measured on each dataset, as the median log ratio of the level-1 value to the calibrated first increment. It is an upper bound, because the increment carries some of the extra charge.

2. What the MIRI images still leave empty¶

A separate analysis (satrestore_tests/holes/) sorted every empty saturated sky pixel of the ten mosaics by why it stayed empty, using the runs of the previous report. Figure 3 shows the share of saturated sky that is restored (light grey) and the empty share by reason. cloudc F2550W and brick have no empty pixels and are left out.

  • Cyan, 77% of the empty area: every group lies above the top of the response curve. The ramp holds no information there, so no ramp method can fill these pixels.
  • Purple, 23%: the curve gives a value, but beyond the range it passed its self-test on (by 0.03–0.4 dex in charge). Extending the curve could reach these, at an untested accuracy.
  • Size: 99% of the empty area lies in regions larger than the 400 pixels the PSF fill accepts. Two regions of ngc6334 F2550W hold 22,782 of its 22,849 empty pixels. Only 3% of the empty area is in regions of 400 pixels or fewer.

Which methods could fill it. The methods were tested by hiding measured pixels around real holes (annuli as wide as the hole radius) and predicting them. Figure 4 gives the rms error per method and dataset. The right column gives the share of empty pixels where at least one other MIRI filter of the same sky has a value.

  • Another filter scaled by the local colour (blue). It reaches 86% of the empty area. It predicts the hidden pixels to an rms of 0.04 dex in gc3571 F1500W and 0.10 dex in ngc6334, the three sets that hold 88% of the empty area. In the smaller F770W and Sgr B2 sets it gives 0.18–0.32 dex, where only one or two other filters exist and their colours vary more.
  • Censored regression on all other filters (orange). This is the W51 model. It is no better in the large sets and much worse where few filters exist: 0.43 dex in sgrb2, 0.46 dex in cloudef, with biases of −0.37 to −0.38 dex.
  • Biharmonic inpainting (grey). It gives 0.10–0.33 dex, and 12–100% of its filled pixels fall below the saturation level, which is impossible for a saturated pixel.
  • Other dithers. They do not help: the mosaic holes are empty in every exposure by construction.
  • Data from other programs. One other program covers 53% of the gc3571 F770W holes, but its values there sit 0.75 dex below the saturation level, so they are themselves unreliable.

These tests sit inside the measured range. Real hole interiors are brighter than any hidden pixel, so the errors inside the holes are expected to be larger.

Methods in the literature (web survey, satrestore_tests/methods_survey/literature.md; reported numbers are from the papers' abstracts and summaries and were not checked in full):

method fills used where notes
other exposures with shorter integration, other filters point and extended Spitzer SMC survey (short exposures); W51 (cross-filter) needs registration and colour scaling
lower-resolution data (Spitzer, WISE, MSX, Herschel) extended, coarse Galactic-plane mosaics needs beam and colour matching; no JWST example found
NIRCam ZEROFRAME point and extended jwst pipeline, for pixels with no good group NIRCam only; frame 0 must not itself be saturated
PSF fit of the wings and spikes point sources Spitzer IRAC (better than 1% for 11 stars), HAWK-I MIRI PSFs broaden by 10–25% for bright stars (brighter-fatter); STPSF does not model this
inpainting (classical or machine-learned) display only cosmic rays, masks invents structure; no photometric use found
persistence in the next exposure no MIRI: under 0.01% after 15–30 min not usable as an estimator

3. The PSF fill¶

A separate study (satrestore_tests/psfbias/) looked for why the PSF fit read too bright at F770W–F2100W. Its findings:

  1. The cached STPSF models already include the detector effects STPSF offers: distortion, the MIRI cruciform up to F1280W, and IPC. Integrating the model over each detector pixel (it is sampled at points) moves values by 0.004–0.02 dex.
  2. The fitting box sets most of the F1500W–F2100W bias. The model's wings beyond a few pixels do not match the data. With a box of 4 pixels around the core instead of 12, PSF−curve at ngc6334 F2100W falls from +0.16 to +0.007 dex.
  3. At F770W the bias comes from the brighter-fatter effect. The self-test bias grows with star brightness (gc3571 F770W: −0.07 to +0.14 dex from the faintest to the brightest quarter of stars). A blur that grows with brightness, plus a calibration against the response curve, brings F770W within 0.05 dex in the study. That adds about 1,800 pixels, but the calibration is fitted on the same curve pixels the gate then checks.

The package takes changes 1 and 2. Figure 5 shows the end-to-end result on the ten datasets: PSF fit against the response curve (left) and the self-test with 7 pixels hidden (right), before (grey) and now (blue). The grey band is the ±0.05 dex gate.

Before, it would have switched on, while the three other F770W sets show the fit 0.13–0.20 dex too bright.

4. The ten MIRI datasets with the final package¶

All ten datasets were rerun with the final package (satrestore_tests/run_sets.sh). The table compares them with the runs of the previous report:

  • the share of saturated sky with a value;
  • the PSF gate;
  • where the level-1 constants came from: own fit or pooled over exposures;
  • the error of the neighbour-flagged level-1 pixels;
  • how many restored sky pixels moved by more than 0.001 dex, and by how much.
In [8]:
def chg(n, v0, sat):
    # restored sky pixels whose value moved by more than 0.001 dex since the previous report, and by how much
    with np.errstate(all='ignore'):
        d = np.abs(np.log10(n / v0))[sat & np.isfinite(n) & np.isfinite(v0)]
    c = d[d > 0.001]
    return {'restored px changed > 0.001 dex': f'{len(c) / max(len(d), 1):.1%}',
            'their median / 95% change (dex)': f'{np.median(c):.4f} / {np.percentile(c, 95):.3f}' if len(c) else '-'}

rows = []

    o, n, m = (fits.getdata(f'{CMP[k]}/{k}_{v}.fits') for v in ['original', 'notrain', 'method'])
    v0 = fits.getdata(f'{CMP[k]}/{k}_notrain_{BEFORE}.fits')
    sat = (m >= 1) & (m <= 6) & np.isnan(o)
    c = S[k]['counts']
    rows.append({'dataset': SETS[k], 'saturated sky px': int(sat.sum()), 'filled before': float(np.isfinite(v0[sat]).mean()),
                 'filled now': float(np.isfinite(n[sat]).mean()), 'PSF fills on': S[k]['psf']['fills_on'],
                 'PSF-filled px (exposures)': int(sum(x['PSF fit'] for x in c)),
                 'level-1 fits: own / pooled': f"{sum(r.get('source') == 'own' for r in S[k]['level1'])} / {sum(r.get('source') == 'pooled' and r['exposure'] != 'all (pooled)' for r in S[k]['level1'])}",
                 'neighbour-flagged level-1 ERR (dex)': round(S[k]['level1_neighbour_flagged']['err'], 3),
                 **chg(n, v0, sat)})
RR = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('dataset')
RR.assign(**{'filled before': RR['filled before'].map('{:.1%}'.format), 'filled now': RR['filled now'].map('{:.1%}'.format)})

5. NIRCam, first version¶

Data. A survey of the disk (satrestore_tests/nircam/) found 256 NIRCam folders, with ramps for most. Six datasets were chosen to cover:

  • readout patterns BRIGHT1, BRIGHT2, SHALLOW2 and SHALLOW4;
  • 2–7 groups and 1–2 integrations;
  • short- and long-wavelength detectors;
  • jwst 1.14 and 1.21.

How NIRCam saturates. Figure 6 shows, for one exposure per dataset, the group in which saturated pixels are first flagged.

  • Group 0 (cyan): 3–20% of the saturated pixels. These have no pipeline value, unless the pipeline computes one from the ZEROFRAME.
  • Group 1 (grey): 23–79% are level-1 pixels.
  • Right column: 58–90% of all saturated pixels are flagged only through a neighbour. After the core saturates, these neighbours collect 12–90% more charge per group.

What differs from MIRI:

  • NIRCam's first group has no pedestal. b is within ±100 DN, against +4,400 for MIRI, and a matches the frame timing (NFRAMES and GROUPGAP) to 3%.
  • NIRCam's raw signal stops rising soon after saturation. A response curve would cover only 1.0–1.3 times the saturation charge, so the package builds none for NIRCam.
  • Group 0 carries per-pixel bias and amplifier offsets in the raw data, so the MIRI raw-to-linearised map does not carry over.

What the first version does:

  • one detector per run;
  • per-pixel saturation levels from the CRDS reference named in each file;
  • the level-1 correction, for ramps of 3 groups or more;
  • the neighbour-flagged level-1 error term;
  • the PSF fill with STPSF models per detector, under the stricter gate (no curve to compare with).

The table summarises the six runs.

  • Level-1 correction: NIRCam's a is close to the pipeline's frame timing, so the correction moves level-1 values by 0.015 dex or less. The 2-group set keeps the pipeline rate.
  • Neighbour-flagged level-1 pixels:
    • the gap to their first increment is small in most sets (−0.014 to −0.089 dex);
    • in the 2-group set it is −0.27 dex, where one long group lets much charge spill;
    • it goes into their ERR.
  • PSF fills: on in W51 F335M and gc2211 F277W, where the worst self-test bin is within 0.02 dex. Off in the other four, where it is 0.024–0.048 dex.
  • omegacen: the level-1 fits of the second integration fail their self-test (half-width 0.2 dex). The package keeps the pipeline rate there.
  • Lost pipeline values: each run now counts them per exposure.
    • Median per exposure: 0–2 in four sets, 23 in omegacen and 390 in gc2211.
    • All come from existing rules: the detector-defect rule (clusters saturated in group 0 in at least 90% of integrations, plus a 2-pixel margin) and, in omegacen, 10 level-1 pixels whose first group is negative.

def nrc_zoom(k, h=45):
    d = f'{O}/nircam_runs/{k}_notrain'
    best = max(SN[k]['counts'], key=lambda x: x['PSF fit'])
    e = best['exposure']
    cal = glob.glob(f'/orange/adamginsburg/jwst/*/*/pipeline/{e}_cal.fits') + glob.glob(f'/orange/adamginsburg/jwst/*/pipeline/{e}_cal.fits')
    o = np.where(fits.getdata(cal[0], 'DQ') & 1, np.nan, fits.getdata(cal[0], 'SCI'))
    with fits.open(f'{d}/{e}_spark.fits') as hh:
        n, m = hh['SCI'].data, hh['METHOD'].data
    lab, nl = ndimage.label(m == 5)
    i = int(np.argmax(ndimage.sum(np.ones_like(m), lab, range(1, nl + 1)))) + 1 if nl else None
    cy, cx = (np.array(np.nonzero(lab == i)).mean(1).astype(int) if i else np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(n), n.shape))
    sl = (slice(max(cy - h, 0), cy + h), slice(max(cx - h, 0), cx + h))
    v = n[sl][np.isfinite(n[sl]) & (n[sl] > 0)]
    norm = LogNorm(np.percentile(v, 5), v.max())
    MC = {0: LIGHT, 1: GREY, 4: EMPTY, 5: ORANGE, 7: RED}
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.8))
    for a_, img, t in [(ax[0], o, f'{NRC[k]}: pipeline'), (ax[1], n, 'JWST-SPARK')]:
        a_.imshow(img[sl], origin='lower', cmap='magma', norm=norm, interpolation='nearest')
        a_.imshow(np.where(np.isnan(img[sl]), 1., np.nan), origin='lower', cmap=ListedColormap([EMPTY]), interpolation='nearest')
        a_.set_title(t); a_.set_xticks([]); a_.set_yticks([]); a_.grid(False)
    mm = m[sl].astype(int)
    ax[2].imshow(np.vectorize(lambda c: list(MC).index(c) if c in MC else 0)(mm), origin='lower', cmap=ListedColormap(list(MC.values())),
                 vmin=-0.5, vmax=len(MC) - 0.5, interpolation='nearest')
    ax[2].set_title('method'); ax[2].set_xticks([]); ax[2].set_yticks([]); ax[2].grid(False)
    fig.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=MC[c], ec=GREY, label=l) for c, l in [(0, 'pipeline'), (1, 'level-1 corrected'), (5, 'PSF fit'),
                                                                        (4, 'not restored'), (7, 'detector defect')]] +
               [Patch(fc=EMPTY, ec=GREY, label='no value (in the images)')], loc='lower center', ncol=6, fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1)); plt.show()

for k in ['w51_F335M_nrcalong', 'brick_F200W_nrca1']:
    nrc_zoom(k)

What the first version leaves out. These are the pieces with the most to gain:

  1. Group 0 of pixels flagged by a neighbour. These are 45–78% of the pixels flagged in group 0, and they have a valid but unlinearised first group. Linearising it needs the per-pixel CRDS linearity coefficients. Those pixels also carry extra charge from their saturated neighbour, so the result needs the same error treatment as section 1.
  2. ZEROFRAME rebuild. The raw ZEROFRAME is valid for 41–82% of the pixels flagged in group 0, but the pipeline zeroes most of them through the neighbour flag. Using it needs the reference-pixel and 1/f corrections the pipeline applies; raw minus superbias leaves 0.1–0.4 dex scatter in brick and Sgr B2.
  3. Cross-filter fill, as for MIRI (section 6).

6. Next steps, by expected gain¶

  1. Cross-filter fill for MIRI. Another filter scaled by the local colour, with the filter chosen by the smallest scatter on the ring and a gate on that scatter.
    • Reaches 86% of the empty area. Tested at 0.04–0.10 dex in the three sets that hold 88% of it.
    • Needs: a new module that takes the restored images of other filters, puts them on each exposure's grid and records the source filter per pixel.
    • Risk: hole interiors are brighter than any tested pixel.
  2. NIRCam group 0 of neighbour-flagged pixels, with the CRDS linearity (section 5, item 1). About half of NIRCam's group-0 pixels.
  3. NIRCam ZEROFRAME rebuild with reference-pixel correction (section 5, item 2).
  4. PSF at F770W: blur that grows with brightness, plus calibration against the curve. About 1,800 pixels in the test sets; needs an independent check of the calibration.
  5. Response curve beyond its tested range. At most 23% of the empty area; its accuracy there is untested.

Appendix: numbers¶

  1. PSF study: the agent's own harness, all variants.
  2. Empty-area categories per dataset, from the mosaics of the previous runs.
  3. Fill-method tests: wide annuli around real holes.
  4. Level-1 tests per dataset:
    • isolated pixels at 4,000–6,000 DN;
    • the neighbour-pixel range;
    • where the served pixels lie.
  5. Level-1 constants and neighbour-flagged error per MIRI dataset (final runs).

Files and commits¶

Package (https://github.com/tyoo37/JWST-SPARK; the W51 copy in satrestore/ follows it):

  • 5298938, bebfd3f: neighbour-flagged level-1 error (code, test, README).
  • 0e1bca2: NIRCam first version.
  • 95f65dd: PSF box 4 px and pixel integration.
  • 7172cb5: level-1 fit gate.
  • daac16d: robust level-1 fit.
  • c77d569: PSF gate on the worst bin; 0.02 dex with no curve.
  • 654889a: pipeline ZEROFRAME rates kept, lost values counted.

Tests and diagnostics (now in git, satrestore_tests/):

  • diag_l1spill.py (section 1);
  • run_sets.sh, run_nircam.sh (reruns);
  • make_report_r2.py, report_r2_text.py (this report).

The studies of sections 2, 3 and 5 are in holes/, psfbias/, methods_survey/ and nircam/, under /orange/adamginsburg/w51/TaehwaYoo/w51_sat_recover/satrestore_tests/.

W51 production (/orange/.../production/miri_ramp):

  • l1nbgap.py writes tables/l1_neighbour_gap.csv;
  • restore.py adds that gap to the ERR of neighbour-flagged level-1 pixels;
  • the earlier products are in restored_before_l1nb_20261031/ and ../final/before_l1nb_20261031/.
